title: R Companion Guide
text:
Preface
This is a guide to learning R. The structure roughly follows the 2nd edition of Statistics Minus the Math: https://minusthemath.com/2e/
Even if you are not using that textbook, you are welcome to use this guide.
Some similar materials are available for learning Stata at the sister site: https://favero-nate.github.io/companion-guides/stata/
If you wish to download a PDF of the text from this guide, one is available here: https://favero-nate.github.io/companion-guides/r/R-Companion-Guide.pdf

title: R Companion Guide
text:
Contents
The main contents of this site will consist of videos you can watch, organized into five parts that can be taught alone or alongside the first several chapters of Statistics Minus the Math. Each part has 3-4 videos.
Below each video, you’ll see a model script, followed by a list of key concepts and syntax that will be helpful to know. However, note that Parts 4-5 are still being created and are currently incomplete.
In the final section of Parts 1-4, I provide an exercise where you can try out what you just learned with a different dataset.

title: R Companion Guide
section: What this guide will and won’t cover
text:
What this guide will and won’t cover
The goal here is dip your toes into the waters of programming in R. Thus, I will provide code that I hope is relatively easy to understand. I will not always follow best practices for coding because I believe doing so sometimes makes the code more difficult for a total beginner. You can learn those best practices later, and there are many great resources available to help (such as R4DS).
As such, I will not teach you to write “good code” (the kind that follows best practices) in these lessons. Instead, I hope you can write code that is good enough to show you some of the power of R and some of the ways data is being processed (without getting too overwhelmed if you are new to programming). Getting this basic familiarity with R will help prepare you to engage with more advanced resources that can teach you to write better code.

title: R Companion Guide
text:
Accessing R
I assume you will be executing R code using Positron or RStudio. You have two options for how to get these programs running:

You can download and install both R and Positron/RStudio on your computer. There are several installation guides available online, such as this one: https://moderndive.com/1-getting-started.html
You can use Positron/RStudio in a web browser through Posit Cloud, which offers free accounts with limited features: https://posit.cloud/

title: Introduction

Key concepts/syntax:

read.csv(): load in a dataset stored in “csv” format
data <- read.csv("https://learndata.net/binge.csv")
View(): show the data in a spreadsheet view
View(data)
referring to variables within a dataset: usually when you refer to a variable you also need to indicate the dataset, sometimes you can use $ to connect the name of the dataset to the name of the variable (column)
data$sex_text
clear out workspace: in RStudio, click the broom icon in the “environment”
To leave a comment in an R script, use #

Comment (or uncomment) several lines in a row: in RStudio, select the lines in the R script you want to modify, and then from the drop-down menu select Code > Comment/Uncomment Lines

title: Variable Types
text:
Key concepts/syntax:

numeric variables: often indicated as num for short, there are many different specific numeric types
character variables: often indicated as chr for short, these are text (non-numeric) variables, also known as string variables
factor variables: sometimes indicated as fct for short, these are qualitative variables that take on specific levels (which can be text) from a finite list
import(): flexible command for loading data files, using the `rio`` package
data <- import("https://learndata.net/binge.Rds", trust = TRUE)
str(): show the variable type for each variable in a dataset
str(data)
levels(): show the levels of a factor variable
levels(data$sex_factor)

title: Put it into Practice
text:
Now it’s time to try things out for yourself. Complete each of the following steps, based on what we learned in this chapter.
Unless your instructor tells you otherwise, use an R script to execute all code needed to accomplish the following:

Load in the social media posts dataset (posts.csv or posts.Rds). You can download it here (csv) or here (Rds) and save it on your computer. Or you can load the file directly into R through the web at the following URL: https://learndata.net/posts.csv


Select four variables to examine. Make sure to choose at least one qualitative (or ordinal) variable and one quantitative variable. Note that binary variables (with values of only 0 and 1) are considered qualitative variables.
For each of these four variables, make at least two graphs. If you are submitting your work to an instructor, you will probably want to save a copy of each graph in a Word document, which you can then submit to show you completed this assignment.
See the video at the bottom of this page for guidance on getting graphs out of R and into a Word doc. You can try using copy-paste. Another option is to take a screenshot and then paste this into your Word doc. One final option (in RStudio) is to click the “Export” button in the Plots window, allowing you to save the graph as its own file in a folder of your choosing; use the “Save as Image” option. In Word, you can then navigate to “insert” a “picture” from your device.

After completing all of this, you should save your R script file in a folder that is convenient to access. It is a good idea at the end of your work to try starting a new R session and then running your entire R script at once, to make sure you have a clean script that can fully execute. If you are submitting work to an instructor, they will likely want you to send them both your script file and a Word doc containing your graphs.

title: File Types

Key concepts:

title: File Types
text:
zip file: a compressed file that can contain several files/folders within it
Excel file: not a plain text file, created for use with Microsoft Excel and uses file ending “.xls” or “.xlsx”
fixed width file: a plain text file format that uses a fixed number of characters for each column (requires access to a dictionary to indicate each column’s width), used to be popular but now less widely used
tab delimited file: a plain text file format that uses tabs to indicate the next column
R file: not a plain text file, created for use with the statistical program R and uses file ending “.Rdata”, “.Rda”, or “.Rds”
Stata data file: not a plain text file, created for use with the statistical program Stata and uses file ending “.dta”
comma delimited file: a plain text file format that uses commas to indicate the next column, can use file ending “.csv”

title: Transforming Variables
text: Model script

title: Transforming Variables
text:
#install.packages("tidyverse")  # uncomment if tidyverse not installed
#install.packages("rio")  # uncomment if rio not installed
library(tidyverse)
library(rio)

data <- import("https://learndata.net/nycschools.dta")

# convert quantitative variables currently
# stored as characters to numbers
data <- data |> mutate(iep = parse_number(iep))
data <- data |> mutate(blackhispanic = parse_number(blackhispanic))
data <- data |> mutate(ell = parse_number(ell))
data <- data |> mutate(thgrmathela = parse_number(thgrmathela))

# rename thgrmathela to something more descriptive
data <- data |> rename(combined_score = thgrmathela)

# log transform the ell variable
data <- data |> mutate(log_ell = log(ell))

# relocate new variable to be next to the original
data <- data |> relocate(log_ell, .after = ell)

# standard ell manually based on summary statistics
#install.packages("psych")  # uncomment if psych not installed
library(psych)
describe(data$ell)
data <- data |> mutate(z_ell = (ell - 13.79) / 12.33)

# drop the standardized variable and then recreate
# it with simpler automated syntax, using scale()
data <- data |> select(!z_ell)
data <- data |> mutate(z_ell = scale(ell))
data <- data |> relocate(z_ell, .after = ell)

title: Transforming Variables
text:
Key concepts/syntax:

|>: this is called a “pipe” (sometimes also written as %>%), here we use it to connect our dataset (data) to a data manipulation function (e.g., mutate(), rename())1
data <- data |> mutate(iep = parse_number(iep))
mutate(): create a new variable (or overwrite an existing one), using the dplyr package which can be loaded in with library(tidyverse)2
data <- data |> mutate(z_ell = (ell - 13.79) / 12.33)
parse_number(): convert a character variable to a numeric one by ignoring all non-numeric characters3
data <- data |> mutate(iep = parse_number(iep))
rename(): rename a variable, using the dplyr package
data <- data |> rename(combined_score = thgrmathela)
log(): a function to create a log transformation (based on the natural log)
data <- data |> mutate(log_ell = log(ell))
relocate(): rearrange the ordering of variables, using the dplyr package
data <- data |> relocate(log_ell, .after = ell)
select(): select only a subset of variables (e.g., all but z_ell), using the dplyr package
data <- data |> select(!z_ell)
!: means “not” (e.g., as is “not this variable”)
data <- data |> select(!z_ell)
scale(): standardize a set of values (e.g., from a variable)
data <- data |> mutate(z_ell = scale(ell))

title: Associations (for Quantitative Variables)
text: Model script

title: Associations (for Quantitative Variables)
text:
#install.packages("tidyverse")  # uncomment if tidyverse not installed
#install.packages("rio")  # uncomment if rio not installed
#install.packages("binsreg")  # uncomment if binsreg not installed
library(tidyverse)
library(rio)
library(binsreg)

# load in and prepare the data
nycschools <- import("https://learndata.net/nycschools.dta")
nycschools <- nycschools |> mutate(thgrmathela = parse_number(thgrmathela))
nycschools <- nycschools |> rename(combined_score = thgrmathela)

# calculate a correlation coefficient
cor(nycschools$overallscore, nycschools$combined_score, use = "complete")

# note that without the proper "use" option, we get
# "NA" as our result due to missing observations
cor(nycschools$overallscore, nycschools$combined_score)

# three different ways to make the same plot
plot(nycschools$combined_score, nycschools$overallscore)
plot(nycschools$overallscore ~ nycschools$combined_score)
plot(overallscore ~ combined_score, data = nycschools)

# add a regression line to the current plot
abline(lm(overallscore ~ combined_score, data = nycschools))

# create a binned scatter plot
binsreg(nycschools$combined_score, nycschools$overallscore)

title: Associations (for Quantitative Variables)
text:
Key concepts/syntax:

cor(): calculate correlations among variables
cor(nycschools$overallscore, nycschools$combined_score, use = "complete")
plot(): create a simple 2D plot, such as a scatter plot
plot(nycschools$combined_score, nycschools$overallscore)
abline(lm()): add a regression line to the current plot
abline(lm(overallscore ~ combined_score, data = nycschools))

title: Regression
text: Model script

title: Regression
text:
#install.packages("tidyverse")  # uncomment if tidyverse not installed
#install.packages("rio")  # uncomment if rio not installed
library(tidyverse)
library(rio)

# load in and prepare the data (using code seen previously)
  data <- import("https://learndata.net/nycschools.dta")
  data <- data |> mutate(iep = parse_number(iep))
  data <- data |> mutate(blackhispanic = parse_number(blackhispanic))
  data <- data |> mutate(ell = parse_number(ell))
  data <- data |> mutate(thgrmathela = parse_number(thgrmathela))
  data <- data |> rename(combined_score = thgrmathela)

# run a regression, then show a summary of its results
regression1 <- lm(overallscore ~ combined_score, data = data)
summary(regression1)

# you can also combine the above into a single line
summary(lm(overallscore ~ combined_score, data = data))

# another regression
regression2 <- lm(overallscore ~ combined_score + ell + iep +
  blackhispanic + economicneedindex, data = data)
summary(regression2)

# if you prefer R to avoid scientific notation (when practical),
# you can change the scipen option in R to a higher value
# (0 is the default; here we set it to 10)
options(scipen = 10)

# now, see how scientific notation is barely used in the results
summary(regression2)

title: Regression
text:
Key concepts/syntax:

lm(): run a linear (OLS) regression
regression1 <- lm(overallscore ~ combined_score, data = data)
summary(): show a summary, such as a summary of regression results
summary(regression1)
options(): change general options in R, such as scientific notation display settings
options(scipen = 10)

title: Qualitative-Qualitative Relationships
text:
Model script
This lesson covers relationships between two categorical (a.k.a., qualitative) variables.

title: Qualitative-Qualitative Relationships
text:
#install.packages("tidyverse")  # uncomment if tidyverse not installed
#install.packages("rio")  # uncomment if rio not installed
#install.packages("gmodels")  # uncomment if gmodels not installed
library(tidyverse)
library(rio)
library(gmodels)

data <- import("https://learndata.net/nycschools.dta")

# basic data processing needed to use this dataset, copied from Ch. 3:
  # convert quantitative variables currently
  # stored as characters to numbers
  data <- data |> mutate(iep = parse_number(iep))
  data <- data |> mutate(blackhispanic = parse_number(blackhispanic))
  data <- data |> mutate(ell = parse_number(ell))
  data <- data |> mutate(thgrmathela = parse_number(thgrmathela))
  
  # rename thgrmathela to something more descriptive
  data <- data |> rename(combined_score = thgrmathela)

# we can use the CrossTable function from gmodels to make crosstabs
# first, we create a table using default settings:
CrossTable(data$schooltype, data$overallgrade)

# the table above is very wide and may be difficult to read
# let's switch the order in which we list our two variable so that
# the variable with more values (overallgrade) will be shown as
# rows rather than columns
CrossTable(data$overallgrade, data$schooltype)

# by default, many proportions are shown below each frequency
# let's turn off all proportions except prop.r (row proportions)
CrossTable(data$overallgrade, data$schooltype, prop.c = FALSE,
  prop.t = FALSE, prop.chisq = FALSE)

# an alternative if we prefer seeing column proportions:
CrossTable(data$overallgrade, data$schooltype, prop.r = FALSE,
  prop.t = FALSE, prop.chisq = FALSE)

# to check for statistical significance, we can set chisq to TRUE:
CrossTable(data$overallgrade, data$schooltype, prop.r = FALSE,
  prop.t = FALSE, prop.chisq = FALSE, chisq = TRUE)

# make a simple bar chart with the ggplot2 package (part of core tidyverse)
data |>
  ggplot(aes(overallgrade)) +
  geom_bar()

# filter out the observations where overallgrade is blank (missing)
data |>
  filter(overallgrade != "") |>
  ggplot(aes(overallgrade)) +
  geom_bar()

# create a grouped bar graph, grouping by schooltype
data |>
  filter(overallgrade != "") |>
  ggplot(aes(overallgrade)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(~ schooltype)

# sometimes it is helpful to adjust the nrow option within
# facet_wrap()
# for example, we can use three rows so our subgraphs are
# shown in a column rather than side-by-side
data |>
  filter(overallgrade != "") |>
  ggplot(aes(overallgrade)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(~ schooltype, nrow = 3)

# alternatively, we can specify two variable within aes():
# grade_factor is shown through the "fill" color while
# schooltype is our main x variable
data |>
  filter(overallgrade != "") |>
  ggplot(aes(fill = overallgrade, x = schooltype)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge")

# change the label (title) for the "fill" legend to "Grade"
data |>
  filter(overallgrade != "") |>
  ggplot(aes(fill = overallgrade, x = schooltype)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
  labs(fill = "Grade")

# we can also display this information in a stacked bar chart
data |>
  filter(overallgrade != "") |>
  ggplot(aes(fill = overallgrade, x = schooltype)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(y = "proportion", fill = "Grade")

title: Qualitative-Quantitative Relationships
text:
Model script
This lesson covers relationships between categorical (a.k.a., qualitative) variables and quantitative variables.

title: Qualitative-Quantitative Relationships
text:
#install.packages("tidyverse")  # uncomment if tidyverse not installed
#install.packages("rio")  # uncomment if rio not installed
#install.packages("psych")  # uncomment if psych not installed
library(tidyverse)
library(rio)
library(psych)

data <- import("https://learndata.net/nycschools.dta")

# basic data processing needed to use this dataset, copied from Ch. 3:
  # convert quantitative variables currently
  # stored as characters to numbers
  data <- data |> mutate(iep = parse_number(iep))
  data <- data |> mutate(blackhispanic = parse_number(blackhispanic))
  data <- data |> mutate(ell = parse_number(ell))
  data <- data |> mutate(thgrmathela = parse_number(thgrmathela))
  
  # rename thgrmathela to something more descriptive
  data <- data |> rename(combined_score = thgrmathela)

# create a table with summary statistics for combined_score by schooltype  
describeBy(data$combined_score, group=data$schooltype)

# an alternative way to create a similar table using tidyverse commands
data |>
  group_by(schooltype) |> 
  summarize(
    n = sum(!is.na(combined_score)),
    mean = mean(combined_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(combined_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(combined_score, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# create a set of box plots showing this same relationship
boxplot(combined_score ~ schooltype, data = data)

# let's use a different qualitative variable (overallgrade)
boxplot(combined_score ~ overallgrade, data = data)

# now recreate the prior boxplot filtering out blanks
# (missing values) before creating the plot
data_nonmissing_grade <- data |> filter(overallgrade != "")
boxplot(combined_score ~ overallgrade, data = data_nonmissing_grade)

title: Regression with Qualitative Variables
text:
Model script
This lesson covers regression with a categorical (a.k.a., qualitative) independent variable.

title: Regression with Qualitative Variables
text:
#install.packages("tidyverse")  # uncomment if tidyverse not installed
#install.packages("rio")  # uncomment if rio not installed
#install.packages("fastDummies")  # uncomment if fastDummies not installed
library(tidyverse)
library(rio)
library(fastDummies)

data <- import("https://learndata.net/nycschools.dta")

# basic data processing needed to use this dataset, copied from Ch. 3:
  # convert quantitative variables currently
  # stored as characters to numbers
  data <- data |> mutate(iep = parse_number(iep))
  data <- data |> mutate(blackhispanic = parse_number(blackhispanic))
  data <- data |> mutate(ell = parse_number(ell))
  data <- data |> mutate(thgrmathela = parse_number(thgrmathela))
  
  # rename thgrmathela to something more descriptive
  data <- data |> rename(combined_score = thgrmathela)

# for a string variable, it can be directly included
# in a regression as a categorical independent variable
summary(lm(combined_score ~ schooltype, data = data))

# if I want more control over how the categorical 
# variable is handled in the regression, I can use
# the fastDummies package to create a set of dummy
# variables from my categorical variable, and then
# I can enter these variables directly into the 
# regression (note: the variable schooltype_K-8 has
# a hyphen in it, which requires referring to it as 
# `schooltype_K-8`)
data <- data |> dummy_cols("schooltype")
summary(lm(combined_score ~ schooltype_Elementary + 
  `schooltype_K-8` + schooltype_Middle, data = data))

# I can see how my results look different if I 
# change the reference category by leaving out one
# category
summary(lm(combined_score ~ schooltype_Elementary + 
  schooltype_Middle, data = data))

# if a categorical variable is stored numerically, it
# will be (incorrectly) treated as a quantitative variable
# by default in a regression:
summary(lm(combined_score ~ district, data = data))

# we can enclose the variable name with factor() so
# R will know to treat the variable as categorical
summary(lm(combined_score ~ factor(district), data = data))

title: Put it into Practice
text:
Now it’s time to try things out for yourself. Complete each of the following steps, based on what we learned in this chapter.
Unless your instructor tells you otherwise, use an R script to execute all code needed to accomplish the following:

title: Put it into Practice
text: This is a modified version of data obtained from Sønderskov and colleagues: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/62BV5 (CC-BY 4.0)↩︎

title: Data Management, Qualitative Dependent Variables
text:
Among other topics, this lesson covers regression with a categorical (a.k.a., qualitative) dependent variable.


 ## Model script
#install.packages("tidyverse")  # uncomment if tidyverse not installed
#install.packages("rio")  # uncomment if rio not installed
#install.packages("fastDummies")  # uncomment if fastDummies not installed
library(tidyverse)
library(rio)
library(fastDummies)

data <- import("https://learndata.net/nycschools.dta")

# basic data processing needed to use this dataset, copied from Ch. 3:
  # convert quantitative variables currently
  # stored as characters to numbers
  data <- data |> mutate(iep = parse_number(iep))
  data <- data |> mutate(blackhispanic = parse_number(blackhispanic))
  data <- data |> mutate(ell = parse_number(ell))
  data <- data |> mutate(thgrmathela = parse_number(thgrmathela))
  
  # rename thgrmathela to something more descriptive
  data <- data |> rename(combined_score = thgrmathela)

# create a factor variable from a string variable
data <- data |>
  mutate(grade_factor = factor(overallgrade, exclude = ""))

# create a table to check mapping of new variable to old one
table(data$overallgrade, data$grade_factor, useNA = "ifany")

data <- data |>
  dummy_cols("overallgrade")

table(data$overallgrade, data$overallgrade_A, useNA = "ifany")

data <- data |>
  select(!overallgrade_:overallgrade_F)

# using the fastDummies package, we can quickly convert a factor
# variable to a set of binary variables (with NAs handled correctly)
data <- data |>
  dummy_cols("grade_factor")

# we can create a table to double-check what the coding looks
# like for one of our new dummy variables
table(data$overallgrade, data$grade_factor_A, useNA = "ifany")

# we can also check how the dummy variable indicating missingness
# is coded:
table(data$overallgrade, data$grade_factor_NA, useNA = "ifany")

# we can also create a binary indicator using mutate() and case_when()
# this approach is more complicated but is flexible and works for
# many recoding tasks
data <- data |>
  mutate(grade_A = case_when(
    overallgrade == "A" ~ 1,
    overallgrade == "" ~ NA,
    .default  = 0
    )
  )

# create a table to check mapping of new variable to old one
table(data$overallgrade, data$grade_A, useNA = "ifany")

# we can also perform ordinary (linear) regression with a dummy
# dependent variable, which is perhaps the simplest way to
# analyze a qualitative dependent variable using regression
summary(lm(grade_factor_A ~ schooltype + combined_score, data = data))

# the regression above showed us predictions for a school
# receiving an overall grade of A; if we want predictions
# for each possible grade, we can run a series of regressions
summary(lm(grade_factor_B ~ schooltype + combined_score, data = data))
summary(lm(grade_factor_C ~ schooltype + combined_score, data = data))
summary(lm(grade_factor_D ~ schooltype + combined_score, data = data))
summary(lm(grade_factor_F ~ schooltype + combined_score, data = data))

# if you want confidence intervals for a regression, you
# can save the result to an object, then use confint()
lm1 <- lm(grade_factor_A ~ schooltype + combined_score, data = data)
confint(lm1)

# by default, 95% confidence intervals are shown, but you
# can change the confidence level
confint(lm1, level = 0.9)
confint(lm1, level = 0.99)

# if we want to run a regression with only elementary schools,
# we can use the filter() function to create a new dataset
# with only this subset of schools, then run our regression
data_elementary <- data |>
  filter(schooltype == "Elementary")
summary(lm(grade_factor_A ~ combined_score, data = data_elementary))

# we can similarly look at non-elementary schools
data_non_elementary <- data |>
  filter(schooltype != "Elementary")
summary(lm(grade_factor_A ~ combined_score, data = data_non_elementary))

title: Instructor Notes
text:
Sample course outline
I’ve constructed this outline to span 10 weeks, since a typical 15 week course on introductory statistics may reserve some weeks for exams or other content.

title: Instructor Notes
text:
Week 1: Getting Started (R Companion Guide Part 1)
Depending on what kind of setup you have for running your software (e.g., in a virtual desktop environment), students may struggle to figure out how to transfer graphs into Word or whatever format you use for student submissions. You may want to walk students through how to do this. You might also want to show students what it means to have a clean script file that will execute in full.


Week 2: Description, File Types (R Companion Guide Part 2)
Especially relevant to this chapter, many students struggle with basic file management. You might want to spend some time showing them what it looks like to have a good folder structure for data work (e.g., using the cloud file storage system provided by your school).


Week 3: Transformations, Associations (R Companion Guide Part 3)
I designed the “Put it into Practice” assignment with the intention that students would get some practice with executing transformations and regressions in software The actual transformations and regression they perform may not be very useful/informative. Still, this exercise can set the scene for a follow-up discussion in class (e.g., comparing regression results from standardized vs. unstandardized variables).


Week 4: Working with Qualitative Variables (R Companion Guide Part 4)
Part 4 starts to introduce some ideas that will require a lot more study to really master. The first section introduces ggplot2, but the grammar of graphics is not really explained because I consider it too complicated for a lesson at this stage. So you may want to emphasize to students that they don’t need to follow the reasoning for all of this code to still make use of it. You might take this opportunity to discuss more generally the process of trying to adapt code chunks you find (e.g., through Google) to your particular project/situation.
In the second section of Part 4, I introduce creating summary tables with the tidyverse, but I also don’t really expect students to be able to generate code like this themselves yet.


Week 5: Data Management and Qualitative Dependent Variables (R Companion Guide Part 5)
The main theme of Part 5 is data management, but that is such a big topic that this coverage is in no way comprehensive. It does fill in several more functions/examples for data manipulation that students may need for simple data projects. Currently, I have not split this up across three pages, but there are three distinct videos that effectively separate the Part 5 model script content into three sections.


Week 6: More Data Visualization (Grammar of Graphics)
The ordering of topics does not follow any particular logic for the five final weeks, so this can be moved around. One potential topic is a more systematic coverage of creating graphs with ggplot2: https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-visualize.html


Week 7: Regression output and robust standard errors
https://evalf21.classes.andrewheiss.com/example/standard-errors/ (if that link ever dies, use the Internet Archive version)


Week 8: Making Nice Tables
There are several packages to choose from, but one option is stargazer. Many introductions are available, but this one from Princeton’s library looks promising (from a quick glance): https://libguides.princeton.edu/R-stargazer


Week 9: R4DS as a Reference Tool
You can assign sections from R4DS that are particularly relevant to whatever you are emphasizing in your class, while more generally discussing how to use the book as a reference tool (e.g., typing a function into the search bar).


Week 10: Plotting Predicted Values from Regression
https://stats.oarc.ucla.edu/r/seminars/interactions-r/
